ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the Earth is located at the center, and orbital lines are drawn near the equator. Point a is on the right side of the Earth's equatorial surface, indicating that it has not yet been launched and rotates together with the Earth; point b is close to the outside of the Earth and is on a near-Earth orbit; point c is on an orbit farther than b; point d is on the outermost orbit, the orbit with the largest radius. The four undergo uniform circular motion around the Earth. Reasoning: The arc length traversed in the same time satisfies s=vt, so it is necessary to compare their respective linear velocities. b, c, and d are circular-orbit satellites orbiting the Earth, and their linear velocities satisfy v=√(GM/r). The smaller the orbital radius r, the greater the linear velocity. In the figure, the orbital radius of b is smaller than those of c and d, so the linear velocity of b is greater than those of c and d. Although a is on the Earth's surface and has a small radius, it is not a free Earth-orbiting satellite, but rotates with the Earth's rotation; the geostationary satellite c has the same angular velocity as the Earth's rotation, so a and c have the same angular velocity. Since the rotation radius of a is smaller than that of c, the linear velocity of a is smaller than that of c. Thus, among the linear velocities, b is the greatest, so the one that traverses the longest arc length in the same time is b.
